First and later pregnancies differ biologically, yet most studies of the maternal and infant
microbiome treat them as interchangeable. My research asks how a mother's pregnancy history and
diet shape the gut and microbiota her child starts life with, and which of those early differences
last into childhood and later life. The work combines human birth cohorts, mouse models of
developmental programming, and methods built for low-biomass and longitudinal microbiome data.

## Pregnancy history and the maternal–infant microbiome

::: {.key-finding}
The maternal gut microbiome adapts differently to a first pregnancy than to later ones, and birth
order shapes neonatal colonization from the first days of life.
:::

First-born children are smaller at birth, one sign that first and later pregnancies differ
biologically. In a prospective cohort at Charité–Universitätsmedizin Berlin, I found that parity
modifies how BMI and gestational weight gain relate to the maternal gut microbiota. Associations
between excess adiposity and community composition were largely confined to first pregnancies,
and multiparous participants followed different microbial trajectories. In a second pregnancy
cohort (Bugs in BHIP), subcommunities of co-occurring taxa expanded and contracted differently in
first and later pregnancies, and their postpartum recovery diverged. Pooling primiparous and
multiparous participants can therefore obscure real biological signal.

The differences extend to the newborn. In neonates, delivery mode, birth order, and sex each
independently shape early colonization, and birth order modifies how delivery mode and
intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) affect colonization in the first days of life. In the
Baby & Mi birth cohort (245 infants, sampled from 3 days to 3 years), I am asking whether these
differences persist through early childhood and whether they track with growth and atopic
outcomes.

::: {.papers}
**Papers:** [Kennedy et al. 2023, *Gut Microbes*](https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2023.2259316) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2025, *Gut Microbes*](https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2025.2491667) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2026, *Gut Microbes*](https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2026.2690907)
:::

## Strain transmission at birth: the Good Bugs Study

Birth-order differences in the infant microbiome are present within the first day of life. Because
the fetal gut has no detectable microbiota before birth, these differences likely arise from what
the mother transmits during delivery. I designed and lead the Good Bugs Study, funded by a
Farncombe Innovation Grant, which uses culture-informed metagenomics to track which maternal
vaginal and gut strains colonize newborns in first and later pregnancies. The study banks isolates
for functional testing, including strains that may limit mother-to-infant transmission of
potential pathogens.

## Maternal diet, the placenta, and the fetal gut

::: {.key-finding}
In mice, maternal high-fat diet disrupts the gut–placenta–fetus axis, and its effects on the
offspring gut persist into adulthood.
:::

My doctoral work used a mouse model of diet-induced obesity to trace how maternal diet affects the
gut–placenta–fetus axis. Characterizing the maternal gut microbiome, maternal intestine, placenta,
and fetal intestine in the same cohort revealed a chain running from diet to fetus: disrupted
maternal intestinal adaptation to pregnancy, placental hypoxia, and altered barrier protein and
immune marker profiles in the fetal gut. That chain is not visible in studies of a single
compartment.

Follow-up work showed that the fetal intestinal inflammation depends on TNF signalling, and that
the effects persist. In adulthood, offspring had altered gut microbiota composition, increased gut
barrier permeability, and greater susceptibility to a postnatal dietary challenge.

::: {.papers}
**Papers:** [Gohir, Kennedy et al. 2019, *J Physiol*](https://doi.org/10.1113/JP277353) ·
PhD thesis, McMaster University, 2021
:::

## Methods for low-biomass and longitudinal data

::: {.key-finding}
Meconium collected before birth has no detectable microbiota, so gut colonization begins at birth.
:::

Reports of bacterial DNA in placenta, amniotic fluid, and meconium suggested that colonization
begins in utero. Most of those studies lacked the contamination controls that low-biomass samples
require. When a sample contains very little microbial DNA, reagent- and laboratory-derived
sequences can dominate the result while still looking biologically plausible. Through a
collaboration with Charité, I applied contamination-aware protocols to meconium collected
immediately before caesarean delivery and found no detectable microbiota. I then re-analysed the
published data behind a high-profile paper that I thought overstated the evidence for fetal
microbial exposure, which became a peer-reviewed letter in *Cell*, and led a *Nature* perspective
with 47 colleagues setting out principles for contamination-aware study design. That attention to
technical artefacts goes back to my MSc work, which showed that PCR amplification introduces
consistent, primer- and region-dependent biases in Illumina-based 16S rRNA gene profiling.

Longitudinal microbiome studies usually track individual taxa or diversity metrics over time. With
McMaster's Department of Mathematics and Statistics, I developed TALDA, which adapts latent
Dirichlet allocation to model subcommunities of co-occurring taxa over time. In the Bugs in BHIP
cohort it detected parity-dependent dynamics that conventional methods missed, and the approach
applies to longitudinal microbiome data well beyond pregnancy.

::: {.papers}
**Papers:** [Kennedy et al. 2021, *Nat Microbiol*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-021-00904-0) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2021, *Cell*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2021.10.026) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2023, *Nature*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-05546-8) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2014, *Appl Environ Microbiol*](https://doi.org/10.1128/AEM.01451-14) ·
[Kennedy et al. 2026, *Gut Microbes*](https://doi.org/10.1080/19490976.2026.2690907)
:::

## From early life to healthspan

The question that runs through all of this work is which early-life differences last, and which
can be changed. The next step is to follow them forward, from childhood growth and allergy to gut
barrier function and health in aging, and to ask where along that path prevention could start.

Early-life programming is well established as a factor in who is susceptible to diet- and
lifestyle-related disease. Whether it also shapes who benefits from interventions, such as changes
in diet or exercise, is largely untested, and the answer could help match prevention to the people
most likely to benefit.
